# Linear Regression in R: Annotated Output

::: notes
Okay! So this talk is a quick dip into some 102-level R. In other words, if you've had a little exposure to R before, such as through an Intro to R for Clinical Data workshop, this is hopefully the right level for you now. 
If you're completely brand new to R, first of all: Welcome! You may find it tricky to actively follow along with the code today since I'm going to skim over some of the initial steps, but go ahead and give it a try, or just listen and watch if that feels more like the right speed. 

Our topic today is linear regression, also called "ordinary least squares (OLS) regression" or sometimes just "the general linear model (GLM)". 
When people say "regression" or "regression model" without any qualifier, this is usually what they're talking about.
It's one of the most widely used statistical models in basically every field and an excellent tool to have at your disposal.

In particular, we're going to dive into some "annotated output"; that means we'll run a regression in R, and then we'll break it down and talk together about each piece of information R spits back at you.
If you've ever run a model in R yourself, or watched someone do it during a workshop, only to find yourself staring blankly at the output and thinking "wait, what?" then I think you'll find this really helpful. 

If you have questions during the talk, feel free to put them in the chat. We have several very friendly R experts on the call today helping out, so they may be able to chime in and answer your questions, otherwise I can.
:::

## What is linear regression good for?

::: {.incremental}

* A single outcome variable that is **continuous**
* One or more predictor variables, continuous or categorical
* The **assumptions** of the general linear model are met -- we'll come back to this

:::

::: notes
Okay, so when might you want to use a linear regression model?
[CLICK]
When you're thinking about which statistical test to use, you're going to need to pay careful attention to which of your variables are *outcomes* vs. *predictors*, and which are *continuous* vs. *categorical*.
As a quick review, categorical variables are variables that have discrete levels, like "what treatment did the patient receive, drug or placebo" or "which department did this encounter take place in". 
With categorical variables, there is no meaning to data in between the levels -- there's no such thing as a patient receiving something halfway between drug and placebo, or having an encounter in something a little more than primary care but a little less than oncology. 
For continuous variables, they're on a scale, and it would be possible to observe data at any point on that scale. 
So something like birth weight would be continuous -- a baby might be born at 7 lbs, or 7.5 lbs, or 7.05 lbs, those all make sense and any value in between them would also make sense. 

[CLICK]

assumption!!

:::

## {{< fa circle-question >}} Troubleshooting

If you make a mistake modifying the data, how can you undo it?

If this were a dataset we read in from an external file (like a .csv), you could just read it in again to get a fresh copy. 
But how do you get a fresh copy of a built-in dataset? 

. . .

To reset the data to its original state, run `rm(msleep)` in the console. This will delete your current version of the data from R's environment, and you'll just be left with the original clean copy from the `ggplot2` package.

::: notes
Remember: If you run `rm(msleep)` to reset the data, you'll need to re-run any changes you made to the data that you want to keep, like converting columns to factor above. 
:::

## {{< fa heart >}} A little encouragement...

**Are these functions new to you? No problem!**

You don't need to understand the underlying statistics for any of these functions to work through the R code and learn from the missingness examples.

::: notes
So if you haven't made a correlation matrix before, or you've never heard of principal components analysis, no worries! That's probably the case for most of the folks here today, so know you're in good company.
We're not going to talk about what these tests are for or what they mean, we're just using them as examples to see different ways of handling missing values.

If you want to learn more about these functions and what they do, click through the links above for explanations and tutorials.
:::



## {{< fa rocket >}} Check your understanding!

<br>

**True or False**: The output from R functions usually tells you how missing data were handled.

{{< fa thumbs-up >}} True!

{{< fa thumbs-down >}} False!

::: notes
Okay! Now we're going to jump into some quick quiz questions to check your understanding. Give me a thumbs-up reaction in Teams if you think this is true and thumbs down if you think it's false: The output from R functions usually tells you how missing data were handled.

False! 
Although some functions, like `geom_point`, provide a warning when dropping missing values, many functions in R do not. We saw an example of this with the `prcomp` function.
:::
